notes.text: The killing and eating of the paschal lamb, ver. 1-6, 8-11.
The sprinkling of the blood upon the doorposts, peculiar to the first passover, ver. 7. with the reason for it, ver. 11-13.

The feast of unleavened bread for seven days after; this points rather at what was to be done after in the observance of this ordinance, ver. 14-20. This institution is communicated to the people, and they instructed in the observance. (1.) Of this first passover, ver. 21-23. (2.) Of the after passovers, ver. 24-27. And the Israelites obedience to these orders, ver. 28. II. None of all the providences of God concerning the Jewish church was more illustrious, than the deliverance of the children of Israel out of Egypt.

1. The first-born of the Egyptians are slain, ver. 29, 30.

2. Orders are given immediately for their discharge, ver. 31-33.

3. They begin their march,

1. Loaded with their own effects, ver. 34.

2. Enriched with the spoils of Egypt, ver. 35, 36.

3. Attended with a mixed multitude, ver. 37, 38,

4. Put to their shifts for present supply, ver. 39. This event is dated, ver. 40-42. III. A recapitulation in the close, 1st. Of this memorable ordinance, with some additions, ver. 43-49; 2ndly. Of this memorable providence, ver. 50, 51.

1. The Lord spake - Had spoken, before the three days darkness. But the mention of it was put off to this place, that the history of the plagues might not be interrupted.

2. This shall be to you the beginning of months - They had hitherto begun their year from the middle of September, but hence-forward they were to begin it from the middle of March, at least in all their ecclesiastical computations. We may suppose that while Moses was bringing the ten plagues upon the Egyptians, he was directing the Israelites to prepare for their departure at an hour's warning. Probably he had, by degrees, brought them near together from their dispersions, for they are here called the congregation of Israel; and to them, as a congregation, orders are here sent.

3. Take every man a lamb - In each of their families, or two or three families, if they were small, join for a lamb. The lamb was to be got ready four days before. and that afternoon they went, they were to kill it, (ver. 6,) as a sacrifice, not strictly, for it was not offered upon the altar, but as a religious ceremony, acknowledging God's goodness to them, not only in preserving them from, but in delivering them by the plagues inflicted on the Egyptians. The lamb so slain they were to eat roasted (we may suppose in its several quarters) with unleavened bread and bitter herbs; they were to eat it in haste, ver. 11, and to leave none of it until the morning; for God would have them to depend upon him for their daily bread. Before they eat the flesh of the lamb, they were to sprinkle the blood upon the door-posts; by which their houses were to be distinguished from the houses of the Egyptians, and so their first-born secured from the sword of the destroying angel. Dreadful work was to be made this night in Egypt; all the first-born both of man and beast were to be slain; and judgment executed upon the gods of Egypt, Num. xxxiii, 4. It is probable the idols which the Egyptians worshipped were defaced, those of metal melted, those of wood consumed, and those of stone broke to pieces. This was to be annually observed as a feast of the Lord in their generations, to which the feast of unleavened bread was annexed, during which, for seven days, they were to eat no bread but what was unleavened, in remembrance of their being confined to such bread for many days after they came out of Egypt, ver. 14- 20. There was much of the gospel in this ordinance: (1.) The paschal lamb was typical. Christ is our passover, 1 Cor. v, 7, and is the Lamb of God, John i, 29. 2. It was to be a male of the first year; in its prime. Christ offered up himself in the midst of his days. It notes the strength and sufficiency of the Lord Jesus, on whom our help was laid. 3. It was to be without blemish, noting the purity of the Lord Jesus, a lamb without spot, 1 Pet. i, 19. 4. It was to be set apart four days before, noting the designation of the Lord Jesus to be a saviour, both in the purpose and in the promise. It is observable, that as Christ was crucified at the passover, so he solemnly entered into Jerusalem four days before, the very day that the paschal lamb was set apart. 5. It was to be slain and roasted with fire, noting the exquisite sufferings of the Lord Jesus, even unto death, the death of the cross. 6. It was to be killed by the whole congregation between the two evenings, that is, between three o'clock and six. Christ suffered in the latter end of the world, Heb. ix, 26, by the hand of the Jews, the whole multitude of them, Luke xxiii, 18. 7. Not a bone of it must be broken, ver. 46, which is expressly said to be fulfilled in Christ, John xix, 33, 36. (2.) The sprinkling of the blood was typical. 1st, It was not enough that the blood of the lamb was shed, but it must be sprinkled, noting the application of the merits of Christ's death to our souls; 2ndly, It was to be sprinkled upon the door-posts, noting the open profession we are to make of faith in Christ, and obedience to him. The mark of the beast may be received in the forehead, or in the right hand, but the seal of the lamb is always in the forehead, Rev. vii, 3. 3rdly, The blood thus sprinkled was a means of the preservation of the Israelites from the destroying angel. If the blood of Christ be sprinkled upon our consciences, it will be our protection from the wrath of God, the curse of the law, and the damnation of hell. (3.) The solemn eating of the lamb was typical of our gospel duty to Christ. 1st, The paschal lamb was killed not to be looked upon only, but to be fed upon; so we must by faith make Christ ours, as we do that which we eat, and we must receive spiritual strength and nourishment from him, as from our food, and have delight in him, as we have in eating and drinking when we are hungry or thirsty. 2ndly, It was to be all eaten: those that, by faith, feed upon Christ, must feed upon a whole Christ. They must take Christ and his yoke, Christ and his cross, as well as Christ and his crown. 3rdly, It was to be eaten with bitter herbs, in remembrance of the bitterness of their bondage in Egypt; we must feed upon Christ with brokenness of heart, in remembrance of sin. 4thly, It was to be eaten in a departing posture ver. 11, when we feed upon Christ by faith, we must sit loose to the world, and every thing in it. (4.) The feast of unleavened bread was typical of the Christian life, 1 Cor. v, 7, 8. Having received Christ Jesus the Lord, 1st. We must keep a feast, in holy joy, continually delighting ourselves in Christ Jesus; If true believers have not a continual feast, it is their own fault. 2ndly, It must be a feast of unleavened bread, kept in charity, without the leaven of malice, and in sincerity, without the leaven of hypocrisy. All the old leaven of sin must be put far from us, with the utmost caution, if we would keep the feast of a holy life to the honour of Christ. 3rdly, It was to be an ordinance forever. As long as we live we must continue feeding upon Christ, and rejoicing in him always, with thankful mention of the great things he has done for us.

glossa.text:
*This month,* etc. ((RAB.)) This is April, which among the Hebrews is called Nisam, among the Macedonians Ξανθικός; and it is called *Aprilis* as it were *aperilis*, because then the earth is opened for the bringing forth of shoots, herbs and flowers: or *Aprilis* from Venus, as it were *Aphroditis*; for Venus in Greek is called *Aphrodite*. The Hebrews hold this month as the first, because the fifteenth of its Kalends was the first day of the world: the fourteenth, the second day; the thirteenth, the third; the twelfth, the fourth, on which the sun and the moon were made, and then was the first equinox; for the sun in the east and the moon in the west divided the sphere of the world equally.

((STRAB.)) This is Nisan, according to the Hebrews, in which the world was made, whose full moon is always to be looked for after the vernal equinox: in which the people of Israel is freed from the servitude of Egypt, and the human race is snatched by the blood of Christ from the power of the devil. On the tenth day of the month the lamb is taken, on the fourteenth it is sacrificed: because in the law the passion of Christ is figured, and, the grace of the Gospel flashing forth, it is fulfilled; for the number ten, because of the decalogue, signifies the law, but the number four the four gospels.

*I have loved.* ((ID.)) This the sheep says which had strayed, the son returned, the pilgrim of this world.

((CASS.)) *I have loved.* Not for the temporal goods given to me, as the unbelievers do, but *because,* etc. God is loved even by unbelievers because he gives good things; whence: *I will praise thee when thou shalt do well to him ((Psal. XLVIII))*. He is loved perfectly, him *eum*; read *cum*, "when" the mind is not moved by adverse things, but is kindled by hope: which manner he afterwards expounds, *I have loved.* Not because he made me a king, or gave me prosperity, but because he hears my prayer in straits.

*And in my days.* ((AUG.)) Namely of my misery, which days I made for myself by sinning, which are full of labour and sorrow, that is, of the old rottenness.

*I will call upon.* Which is not without faith; whence the Apostle: *How shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? ((Rom. X.))* When therefore he says, *they shall call upon,* note that the lover is not idle. In which, *They have compassed me,* etc. Or, in the days of salvation, that is, in the time of fulness; whence: *Behold, now is the acceptable time,* etc. ((II Cor. VI)).

notes.text: I received — By an immediate Revelation.

This is my body, which is broken for you — That is, this broken bread is the sign of my body, which is even now to be pierced and wounded for your iniquities. Take then, and eat of, this bread, in an humble, thankful, obediential remembrance of my dying love; of the extremity of my sufferings on your behalf, of the blessings I have thereby procured for you, and of the obligations to love and duty which I have by all this laid upon you.

After supper — Therefore ye ought not to confound this with a common meal. Do this in remembrance of me - The ancient sacrifices were in remembrance of sin: this sacrifice, once offered, is still represented in remembrance of the remission of sins.
Ye show forth the Lord's death — Ye proclaim, as it were, and openly avow it to God, and to all the world. Till he come - In glory.

glossa.text: *For I have received,* etc. He shows that the mystery of the Eucharist, celebrated in the midst of supping, is not the supper. For it is a spiritual medicine, and the memory of our redemption, that we may obtain greater things, because by the death of Christ we have been freed. Of this we ought to be mindful in eating and in drinking, having obtained the New Testament herein: because the blood is the witness of the divine benefit, whence we receive it for the protection of body and of soul: because the flesh of Christ is for the health of the body, the blood for our soul: and therefore the law foretold that blood was not to be eaten. *In the night wherein.* Having suffered in the night, he came to the light of the resurrection.

*He broke.* In the sacrament, namely, according to what was seen and was believed by the faithful to be also whole. He gave one to all, that they might remain in unity: but when he broke it, he showed his voluntary passion.
*As often as.* He expounds unto what commemoration of Christ, namely, his death. *Until he come.* Because this will not be changed, as were the sacraments of the Jews.

notes.text: Before the feast — Namely, on Wednesday, in the paschal week. Having loved his own - His apostles, he loved them to the end - Of his life.
Jesus knowing — Though conscious of his own greatness, thus humbled himself.
Layeth aside his garments — That part of them which would have hindered him.
Into the basin — A large vessel was usually placed for this very purpose, wherever the Jews supped.

What I do thou knowest not now; but thou shalt know hereafter — We do not now know perfectly any of his works, either of creation, providence, or grace. It is enough that we can love and obey now, and that we shall know hereafter.

If I wash thee not — If thou dost not submit to my will, thou hast no part with me - Thou art not my disciple. In a more general sense it may mean, If I do not wash thee in my blood, and purify thee by my Spirit, thou canst have no communion with me, nor any share in the blessings of my kingdom.
Lord, not my feet only — How fain would man be wiser than God! Yet this was well meant, though ignorant earnestness.
And so ye, having been already cleansed, need only to wash your feet — That is, to walk holy and undefiled.
The servant is not greater than his Lord — Nor therefore ought to think much of either doing or suffering the same things.

glossa.text: *That he should pass.* The evangelist interprets for us the name of the pasch, that is, a passing over, and its signification: because as they passed out of Egypt, so Christ out of the world. So we also, marked with the blood of the Lamb, from vices to virtues, from the world to heaven. *He loved them unto the end.* Unto the end, that is, unto Christ who is the consummating end, that is, that by love of him they may pass whither he himself passes. Or unto the end, that is, unto death: not that his love is ended by death, but that he loved so far that love led him even unto death, wherein he gave an example that all should remain in the truth of God unto the end.

*And when supper was done.* The supper signifies the passion. For as after supper there is no dinner, so also Christ, after he has once suffered, does not suffer again. He rises from supper; after the passion he lays aside his garments; according to his former infirmity he girded himself with a linen cloth, his flesh being now immortal; he puts water into a basin, that is, the grace of baptism; he washes the feet and wipes them from sins in baptism; *he took his garments,* that is, the Jews at the end of the world, whom he had first laid aside as blinded.

*He riseth from supper.* From that heavenly refreshment with which he was refreshed among the angels he lays aside his garments, the glory of eternal blessedness. *And layeth aside his garments.* He passed over his loftiness, being about to place his lowliness beneath it, that lowliness might be perfectly commended to man, since one so lofty humbled himself so far that he washed even the feet of the traitor.
*After that he putteth.* He poured his blood upon the earth, that he might cleanse the steps of believers, which were soiled with earthly sins.

*Peter saith to him,* etc. Because of the loftiness of the promised mystery he does not yet permit it to be done; he cannot yet endure that God be humbled at his feet, being struck through with dread. *He answered.* He who is not washed through baptism and the confession of penance has no part with Jesus.

*Simon saith to him.* Peter's error here profited us. For he erred that we might not err. He erred when he offered his whole self to God to be washed, whom God corrected, showing that one once baptized is not to be baptized again.

*He that is washed.* From these words we understand that the apostles were baptized, although we do not read where or when. *He that is washed.* He that is washed by baptism is clean. But because he is again soiled by the dust of his earthly dwelling, there is again need to wash the feet, which the Lord washes by interceding for us, and we ourselves by praying. He also who in leisure studies the truth, while he goes to open to the bridegroom knocking in others, soils his feet, because the truth is heard humbly, but cannot be preached without danger; but these feet the Lord washes for his disciples.

*And when he had sat down, he said to them again: Know you what I have done to you? You call me,* etc. As before by example, so now also by word the master of truth instructs them. And that he says great things of himself is not arrogance, but truth which profits the hearers, as Paul also does.

((GREG.)) Incautious are the humble who ensnare themselves in a lie while they shun arrogance, because they set themselves against the truth which they forsake. For he who under compelling necessity speaks true and good things of himself is joined so much the more to humility as he is allied to truth.

echoes.text: Moses took the blood, and sprinkled it on the people, and said, “Look, this is the blood of the covenant, which Yahweh has made with you concerning all these words.”
echoes.note: 'This cup is the new covenant in my blood' (v.25) fuses Moses' words at Sinai, 'the blood of the covenant,' with covenant-inauguration sacrifice. High volume via the covenant+blood pairing and strong coherence; the Supper is presented as a covenant-ratifying meal.

echoes.text: Behold, the days come, says Yahweh, that I will make a new covenant with the house of Israel, and with the house of Judah:
echoes.note: The phrase 'the new covenant' (v.25) is verbatim from Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant (LXX Jer 38:31). Highest volume of any echo here; Jesus' cup-word interprets the Supper as the inauguration of Jeremiah's promised covenant.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: The institution 'on the night in which he was betrayed' (v.23) over bread and cup is set within the Passover frame; the memorial meal ('in memory of me') echoes the Passover's perpetual remembrance. Coherence is strong, though the verbal overlap is thematic rather than quoted.

echoes.text: This day shall be to you for a memorial, and you shall keep it a feast to Yahweh: throughout your generations you shall keep it a feast by an ordinance forever.
echoes.note: 'Do this in memory of me' (vv.24-25) mirrors the Passover ordinance that the day be a 'memorial' (zikkaron / LXX mnemosynon) kept perpetually. The memorial-meal logic transfers from Exodus to the Lord's Supper.

echoes.text: As for you also, because of the blood of your covenant, I have set free your prisoners from the pit in which is no water.
echoes.note: 'By the blood of your covenant I have set your prisoners free' is one possible background for 'the new covenant in my blood' (v.25), linking covenant blood to liberation. Faint and secondary to Exodus 24/Jeremiah 31; low volume.

echoes.text: Therefore will I divide him a portion with the great, and he shall divide the plunder with the strong; because he poured out his soul to death, and was numbered with the transgressors; yet he bore the sin of many, and made intercession for the transgressors.
echoes.note: The body 'which is for you' and proclaiming the Lord's death (vv.24, 26) may echo the Servant who 'poured out his soul to death' and bore others' sin. Low volume, contested; resonance is conceptual rather than verbal in this passage.

echoes.attribution: Catena, CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wilson Pruitt / Wroot Press)

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, “This month shall be to you the beginning of months. It shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak to all the congregation of Israel, saying, ‘On the tenth day of this month, they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to their fathers’ houses, a lamb for a household; and if the household is too little for a lamb, then he and his neighbor next to his house shall take one […]
echoes.note: John frames the entire farewell on the eve of 'the feast of the Passover,' deliberately situating Jesus' self-giving against the exodus deliverance. Volume and coherence are high in John, which has already cast Jesus as the lamb (1:29) and dates the crucifixion to Passover. The footwashing supper thus becomes the new Passover meal of departure.

echoes.text: There was given him dominion, and glory, and a kingdom, that all the peoples, nations, and languages should serve him: his dominion is an everlasting dominion, which shall not pass away, and his kingdom that which shall not be destroyed.
echoes.note: 'The Father had given all things into his hands' echoes the giving of universal dominion to the one like a son of man. The handing-over language coheres with John's repeated Son-of-Man glorification motif and prepares for 13:31. Coherence is strong though the wording is general.

echoes.text: You make him ruler over the works of your hands. You have put all things under his feet:
echoes.note: 'All things into his hands' may echo the psalmist's 'you put all things under his feet/gave him dominion.' The thought-rhyme of universal subjection is present but the verbal overlap is faint and the motif is widely diffused.

echoes.text: Yahweh appeared of old to me, saying, Yes, I have loved you with an everlasting love: therefore with loving kindness have I drawn you.
echoes.note: 'Having loved his own... he loved them to the end' resonates with the LORD's everlasting love and faithful hesed toward his own people. The covenant-love register fits, but the wording is too common to claim a deliberate citation.

echoes.text: Satan stood up against Israel, and moved David to number Israel.
echoes.note: 'The devil having already put into the heart of Judas to betray him' echoes the Satan who 'stood up against Israel and incited David.' The pattern of the adversary inciting a human agent to a destructive deed coheres with the fuller 'Satan entered into him' of 13:27. Availability and recurrence in Second-Temple Satan-tradition support the link.

echoes.text: Now on the day when God’s sons came to present themselves before Yahweh, Satan also came among them. Yahweh said to Satan, “Where have you come from?” Then Satan answered Yahweh, and said, “From going back and forth in the earth, and from walking up and down in it.” Yahweh said to Satan, “Have you considered my servant, Job? For there is no one like him in the earth, a blameless and an upright man, one who fears God, and turns away from evil.” Then Satan […]
echoes.note: The accuser figure who provokes harm against the righteous undergirds the Johannine 'devil.' The connection is thematic rather than verbal and the Job satan is a heavenly prosecutor, so the echo is faint.

echoes.text: Now let a little water be fetched, wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree.
echoes.note: Abraham's 'let a little water be brought and wash your feet' establishes footwashing as the host's act of hospitality, here inverted so the Lord performs the servant's task. The image is the closest patriarchal antecedent and coheres with John's reversal of status. Recurrence of the motif across Genesis strengthens availability.

echoes.text: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
echoes.note: Abigail's 'a servant to wash the feet of my lord's servants' marks footwashing as the lowliest slave duty. Jesus assuming exactly this office dramatizes 13:16 (the servant not greater than his lord). The status-coherence is strong.

echoes.text: Aaron and his sons shall wash their hands and their feet in it. When they go into the Tent of Meeting, they shall wash with water, that they not die; or when they come near to the altar to minister, to burn an offering made by fire to Yahweh. So they shall wash their hands and their feet, that they not die: and it shall be a statute forever to them, even to him and to his descendants throughout their generations.”
echoes.note: The priestly laver where Aaron and his sons wash hands and feet to be clean for service frames footwashing as cultic purification for ministry. Jesus' 'if I don't wash you, you have no part with me' reads the act as priestly consecration. Coherence with the cleansing language is high.

echoes.text: Yahweh spoke to Moses and to Aaron, saying, “This is the statute of the law which Yahweh has commanded. Tell the children of Israel to bring you a red heifer without spot, in which is no defect, and which was never yoked. You shall give her to Eleazar the priest, and he shall bring her outside of the camp, and one shall kill her before his face. Eleazar the priest shall take some of her blood with his finger, and sprinkle her blood toward the front of the […]
echoes.note: The water of purification that cleanses defilement supplies the conceptual background for 'completely clean.' The transfer from ritual to christological cleansing fits John's pattern of fulfilling purification rites. The link is conceptual, not verbal.

echoes.text: Purify me with hyssop, and I will be clean. Wash me, and I will be whiter than snow.
echoes.note: 'Wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow' supplies the imagery of moral cleansing behind 'you are clean.' The penitential washing register coheres with Jesus distinguishing the bathed-and-clean from the betrayer. Wording overlaps in the wash/clean pairing.

echoes.text: I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean: from all your filthiness, and from all your idols, will I cleanse you.
echoes.note: 'I will sprinkle clean water on you, and you shall be clean' is the eschatological cleansing promise most verbally aligned with 'you are clean.' Its new-covenant context coheres with the new commandment of 13:34. Volume of the clean-water motif raises confidence.

echoes.text: “In that day there will be a spring opened to the house of David and to the inhabitants of Jerusalem, for sin and for uncleanness.
echoes.note: The fountain opened 'for sin and for impurity' supplies an eschatological cleansing backdrop. The connection is thematic and the wording does not closely match. Marked faint.

echoes.text: How beautiful on the mountains are the feet of him who brings good news, who publishes peace, who brings good news of good, who publishes salvation, who says to Zion, “Your God reigns!”
echoes.note: The 'beautiful feet' of the herald is sometimes invoked behind footwashing, but the link is associative only and the volume is negligible. Listed for completeness and marked contested.

echoes.text: She arose, and bowed herself with her face to the earth, and said, “Behold, your handmaid is a servant to wash the feet of the servants of my lord.”
echoes.note: 'A servant is not greater than his lord' restates the lord/servant hierarchy that Abigail's footwashing self-description presumes, now made the basis for mutual service. The status logic coheres tightly with the preceding act. Recurrence of the master/servant ordering across the OT supports availability.

echoes.text: Abraham said to his servant, the elder of his house, who ruled over all that he had, “Please put your hand under my thigh.
echoes.note: 'One who is sent is not greater than he who sent him' reflects the shaliach principle dramatized by Abraham's commissioned servant who acts with his master's authority. The agency concept is Second-Temple and pervasive, so the echo is conceptual and faint.

echoes.text: Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers;
echoes.note: 'Blessed are you if you do them' adopts the OT beatitude form that ties blessing to doing the will/law. The macarism cadence is biblical but generic, so the link is to a form rather than a text.

harmony.title: The Last Supper
harmony.note: The Synoptics give the bread and the cup; John gives the footwashing in their place. The Synoptics call it the Passover; John times the death to the Passover lambs instead — the gospels' hardest chronological knot.

harmony.title: The footwashing and farewell discourse
harmony.note: Five chapters where the Synoptics give the meal: the new commandment, the vine, the Paraclete, and the high-priestly prayer. John only.

lines: He rises from supper, ties the towel, and kneels.
He washes our feet and bids us do the same.
He takes the bread, the cup of salvation.
This is his body and his blood, given for us.
A new commandment he gives us this night.
Love one another as I have loved you. Come, let us worship.

registers.label: Immersive
lines: Feel the warm water poured over tired feet, the towel at his waist, the Lord of all kneeling on the floor.
Love one another as I have loved you.
This is the night of the lamb and the blood on the door, the night God passed over and led the people out.
Love one another as I have loved you.
He takes the bread and gives thanks; he lifts the cup of salvation and calls on the name of the Lord.
Love one another as I have loved you.
Do this in remembrance of me, he says, and stoops once more to serve. Come, let us worship.
Love one another as I have loved you. Amen.
